```{r setup, include=FALSE}
# This chunk loads libraries and prepares all data for the plots and tables.
# It will not be shown on the final webpage.

# 1. LOAD LIBRARIES
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(gt)
library(scales)
library(sf)
library(leaflet)
library(ggiraph) 

# 2. LOAD DATA
vz_data <- read_csv(here::here("data", "input", "intersection_intervention_table_ever_treated_2015-2022.csv"))

# 3. PREPARE DATA FOR PLOT 1: Total Pedestrian Casualties by Year
casualties_by_year <- vz_data %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarise(total_casualties = sum(pedestrian_death_or_injury, na.rm = TRUE))

# 4. PREPARE DATA FOR THE FACETED CASUALTY TRENDS PLOT
casualties_by_intervention_group <- vz_data %>%
  select(intersection_id, year, pedestrian_death_or_injury, ends_with("_post")) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(ends_with("_post"), -covid_pre_post),
    names_to = "intervention_type",
    values_to = "is_active"
  ) %>%
  group_by(intervention_type, intersection_id) %>%
  mutate(was_ever_treated = max(is_active)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  filter(was_ever_treated == 1) %>%
  group_by(intervention_type, year) %>%
  summarise(total_casualties = sum(pedestrian_death_or_injury, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(
    intervention_type = str_replace_all(intervention_type, "_post", ""),
    intervention_type = str_replace_all(intervention_type, "_", " "),
    intervention_type = str_to_title(intervention_type)
  )

# 5. PREPARE DATA FOR PLOT 2: First-time Interventions (ANY type) by Year
first_treatment_year <- vz_data %>%
  mutate(treatment_count = select(., ends_with("_post")) %>% 
                           select(-speed_limit_post) %>% 
                           rowSums(na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  filter(treatment_count > 0) %>%
  group_by(intersection_id) %>%
  summarise(first_year = min(year, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  ungroup()

interventions_by_year <- first_treatment_year %>%
  count(first_year, name = "num_intersections")

# 6. PREPARE DATA FOR THE NINE SMALL PLOTS: First year for EACH intervention type
first_year_by_intervention <- vz_data %>%
  select(intersection_id, year, ends_with("_post")) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(ends_with("_post"), -covid_pre_post),
    names_to = "intervention_type",
    values_to = "is_active"
  ) %>%
  filter(is_active == 1) %>%
  group_by(intersection_id, intervention_type) %>%
  summarise(first_year = min(year), .groups = "drop") %>%
  count(intervention_type, first_year, name = "num_intersections") %>%
  mutate(
    intervention_type = str_replace_all(intervention_type, "_post", ""),
    intervention_type = str_replace_all(intervention_type, "_", " "),
    intervention_type = str_to_title(intervention_type)
  )

# 7. PREPARE DATA FOR THE RESULTS TABLE
regression_results_detailed <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Intervention, ~IRR, ~CI_Lower, ~CI_Upper, ~P_Value,
  "Street Improvement Project Intersection", 1.118, 0.958, 1.305, 0.156,
  "25 MPH Signal Retiming", 1.071, 1.026, 1.118, 0.002,
  "Leading Pedestrian Interval Signal", 1.042, 0.992, 1.095, 0.102,
  "Enhanced Crossing", 1.000, 0.765, 1.308, 0.999,
  "Street Improvement Project Corridor", 0.951, 0.909, 0.995, 0.029,
  "Citywide Speed Limit Reduction", 0.945, 0.900, 0.992, 0.021,
  "Speed Hump", 0.885, 0.815, 0.962, 0.004,
  "Turn Traffic Calming", 0.856, 0.779, 0.941, 0.001,
  "Neighborhood Slow Zone", 0.816, 0.691, 0.964, 0.017
) %>%
  mutate(
    Percent_Change = (IRR - 1),
    CI_Percent_Formatted = paste0(
      "[",
      scales::percent((CI_Lower - 1), accuracy = 0.1),
      ", ",
      scales::percent((CI_Upper - 1), accuracy = 0.1),
      "]"
    )
  )

# 8. PREPARE DATA FOR THE DESCRIPTIVE TABLE
intervention_descriptions <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Intervention, ~Description, ~`Components/ Examples`,
  "Citywide Speed Limit Reduction", "Default speed limit change from 30 MPH to 25 MPH.", "Streets may be signed or unsigned.",
  "Enhanced Crossing", "A marked high-visibility crosswalk on calm streets with low vehicle volumes, high pedestrian traffic, and no traffic signal or stop sign.", "At minimum, include high visibility crosswalk markings, daylighting on all approaches, Americans with Disabilities Act compliant pedestrian ramps, and pedestrian warning signage.",
  "Leading Pedestrian Interval Signal", "Signals that show a pedestrian walk sign before showing a green light to vehicle traffic in the same direction, giving pedestrians a head start to cross the street before car traffic.", NA,
  "Neighborhood Slow Zone", "Neighborhood areas, selected based on crashes, presence of schools, and other factors, in which the speed limit has been reduced to 20 mph.", "Include road markings and signs indicating entrance to a slow zone, along with greater concentration of other interventions.",
  "SIP Corridors", "Safety-oriented engineering improvements that use multiple treatments in a street corridor.", "Examples: large range of subtypes, including markings, vertical elements, signage and regulatory changes, signal changes, concrete, and landscaping.",
  "SIP Intersection", "Safety-oriented engineering improvements that use multiple treatments in a single intersection.", "Same as above, but within intersections rather than along street corridors.",
  "Speed Hump", "A raised area of a roadway designed to reduce vehicle speeds.", NA,
  "Turn Traffic Calming", "A traffic calming measure that guides drivers to turn more safely and increases pedestrian visibility.", "Examples: hardened centerline, slow turn wedge, bike island channelization, median extension.",
  "25 MPH Signal Retiming", "A corridor where the signal progression has been changed to match the 25 MPH speed limit.", NA
)

# 9. Prep for plot-effects
results_with_color <- regression_results_detailed %>%
  mutate(
    Significance = case_when(
      P_Value <= 0.05 & Percent_Change < 0 ~ "Significant Reduction",
      P_Value <= 0.05 & Percent_Change > 0 ~ "Significant Increase",
      TRUE ~ "Not Significant"
    )
  )
```

::::::::: grid
::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-8}
# Evaluating the Impact of Vision Zero Interventions on Pedestrian Casualties in NYC (2013-2023)

Motor vehicle crashes are a leading cause of death and injury in New York City (NYC). In 2014, the city adopted the **Vision Zero (VZ)** framework, a comprehensive strategy to eliminate all traffic-related fatalities. The program uses a multi-faceted approach, including infrastructure redesign, lower speed limits, and public awareness campaigns. This analysis evaluates the impact of nine distinct street-level interventions on pedestrian casualties. The study examines data from 2013 to 2023, focusing specifically on intersections that received treatments between 2015 and 2021. This approach ensures that every intervention can be evaluated with at least two years of 'before' data and two years of 'after' data, allowing for a robust comparison.
:::

::::::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-4}
:::::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
Key Findings

::: key-finding
<i class="fas fa-check-circle"></i> **Speed is Key** <br> Interventions that physically slow traffic, like **Neighborhood Slow Zones (-18%)**, were most effective.
:::

::: key-finding
<i class="fas fa-times-circle"></i> **Unintended Harm** <br> **Signal Retiming** to improve vehicle flow was linked to a **7% increase** in casualties.
:::

::: key-finding
<i class="fas fa-minus-circle"></i> **Mixed Results** <br> Other common treatments showed no significant citywide impact on pedestrian safety.
:::
::::::
:::::::
:::::::::

### What Are the Vision Zero Interventions?

The analysis focuses on nine key physical and regulatory changes made to NYC streets. The table below provides a brief description of each intervention.

```{r table-descriptions, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
intervention_descriptions %>%
  gt() %>%
  fmt_markdown(columns = everything()) %>%
  cols_width(
    Intervention ~ px(180),
    Description ~ px(350),
    everything() ~ px(300)
  ) %>%
  cols_label(
    `Components/ Examples` = "Components / Examples"
  ) %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "Descriptions of Assessed Vision Zero Interventions"
  ) %>%
  tab_options(
    column_labels.font.weight = "bold"
  )
```

### Map of All Vision Zero Interventions

::::: grid
::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-3}
-   The interactive map on the right displays the polygon geometry for every intersection in NYC. Zoom-in and click on any intersection to see a list of the Vision Zero interventions it has received and the year each was first implemented.

-   **Note**: This map displays ALL intersections in the city, including ones which were left out of our statistical modeling.
:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-9}
```{r intersection-map}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| cache: true

# --- Step 1 & 2: Load and Prepare Popup Data ---
full_geo_data <- read_csv(here::here("data", "input", "intersection_intervention_table_final_w_geo.csv"))

intervention_name_map <- c(
  "leading_pedestrian_interval_post" = "Leading Pedestrian Interval",
  "turn_traffic_calming_post" = "Turn Traffic Calming",
  "enhanced_crossing_post" = "Enhanced Crossing",
  "speed_humps_post" = "Speed Humps",
  "street_improvement_project_post" = "SIP Intersection",
  "street_improvement_corridors_post" = "SIP Corridor",
  "signal_retiming_post" = "25 MPH Signal Retiming",
  "slow_zones_post" = "Neighborhood Slow Zone",
  "speed_limit_post" = "Citywide Speed Limit Reduction"
)

popup_summary <- full_geo_data %>%
  select(intersection_id, year, ends_with("_post"), -covid_pre_post) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -c(intersection_id, year),
    names_to = "intervention_type",
    values_to = "is_active"
  ) %>%
  filter(is_active == 1) %>%
  group_by(intersection_id, intervention_type) %>%
  summarise(first_year = min(year), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(intervention_name = recode(intervention_type, !!!intervention_name_map)) %>%
  mutate(popup_line = paste0("<b>", intervention_name, ":</b> ", first_year)) %>%
  group_by(intersection_id) %>%
  summarise(
    popup_html = paste0(popup_line, collapse = "<br>")
  ) %>% 
  mutate(popup_html = if_else(is.na(popup_html), "No VZ interventions recorded.", popup_html))

# --- Step 3: Create a unique spatial dataset with Polygons ---
intersections_sf <- full_geo_data %>%
  select(intersection_id, intersection_geom) %>%
  tidyr::drop_na(intersection_geom) %>%
  distinct(intersection_id, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  st_as_sf(wkt = "intersection_geom", crs = 2263) %>%
  st_transform(crs = 4326)

# --- Step 4: Join popup data to the spatial data ---
intersections_for_map <- intersections_sf %>%
  left_join(popup_summary, by = "intersection_id")

# --- Step 4.5: Create a separate dataset for the circle markers ---
intersections_centroids <- intersections_for_map %>%
  st_centroid()

# --- Step 5: Build the Leaflet Map with Correct Data for Each Layer ---
leaflet() %>%
  addProviderTiles(providers$CartoDB.Positron, group = "Basemap") %>%
  setView(lng = -74.00, lat = 40.71, zoom = 11) %>%
  
  # Circles Layer
  addCircles(
    data = intersections_centroids,
    radius = 5, # Radius is now in METERS
    stroke = FALSE,
    fillColor = "#E37222", 
    fillOpacity = 0.7,
    popup = ~popup_html,
    group = "Overview (Circles)"
  ) %>%
  
  # Polygons layer 
  addPolygons(
    data = intersections_for_map,
    fillColor = "#05014a", 
    fillOpacity = 0.5,
    stroke = TRUE,
    color = "#FFFFFF",
    weight = 0.5,
    popup = ~popup_html,
    group = "Detailed (Shapes)"
  ) %>%
  
  # Layer Control 
  addLayersControl(
    baseGroups = c("Overview (Circles)", "Detailed (Shapes)"),
    options = layersControlOptions(collapsed = FALSE)
  )
```
:::
:::::

### Citywide Pedestrian Casualty Trends

To understand the citywide context, we first examined the overall trend in pedestrian casualties across all 9,562 intersections in our study.

::::: grid
::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6}
-   **The number of pedestrian casualties showed a general downward trend** over the study period, with a sharp, anomalous drop in 2020. This dip corresponds to the major changes in traffic patterns and pedestrian activity during the first year of the COVID-19 pandemic.

-   **While casualties rebounded after 2020, they remained below pre-pandemic levels**, suggesting that Vision Zero initiatives may be contributing to a sustained, long-term improvement in pedestrian safety.
:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6}
```{r plot-casualties, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
# Step 1: Pre-calculate the tooltip column
casualties_by_year <- casualties_by_year %>%
  mutate(tooltip_text = paste("Year:", year, "<br>Total Casualties:", comma(total_casualties)))

# Step 2: Create the plot. Move interactive aes to the geom that needs it.
p <- ggplot(casualties_by_year, aes(x = year, y = total_casualties, group = 1)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1.2) + # Standard, non-interactive line
  geom_point_interactive(aes(tooltip = tooltip_text, data_id = year), color = "steelblue", size = 3) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2013, 2023, by = 2)) +
  labs(
    title = "Annual Pedestrian Casualties in Study Sample",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Total Pedestrian Casualties"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

# Step 3: Render with girafe() and print the object
g <- girafe(
  ggobj = p,
  options = list(
    opts_tooltip(
      opacity = 0.8,
      css = "background-color:black; color:white; padding:10px; border-radius:5px; font-family:sans-serif;"
    ),
    opts_toolbar(saveaspng = TRUE)
  )
)
g
```
:::
:::::

### Vision Zero Implementation Timeline

The Vision Zero program was rolled out in a staggered fashion, with different intersections receiving treatments in different years. Our study design leverages this staggered implementation to better isolate the causal impact of each intervention.

::::: grid
::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6}
-   **Nearly 25% of intersections in our data received their first Vision Zero intervention in 2016,** with 2,247 intersections treated during that year.

-   **No intersection in our data received its first Vision Zero treatment in 2021**, suggesting that the program's implementation to *new* intersections might have been limited in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic.
:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6}
```{r plot-interventions, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
# Plot and display
interventions_by_year <- interventions_by_year %>%
  mutate(tooltip_text = paste("Year:", first_year, "<br>New Intersections:", comma(num_intersections)))
p <- ggplot(interventions_by_year, aes(x = first_year, y = num_intersections)) +
  geom_col_interactive(aes(tooltip = tooltip_text, data_id = first_year), fill = "darkorange", alpha = 0.9) +
  geom_text(aes(label = comma(num_intersections)), vjust = -0.5, size = 3.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma, expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.1))) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2015:2021) +
  labs(
    title = "Intersections Receiving First VZ Treatment",
    subtitle = "Excludes universal 2014 speed limit reduction",
    x = "Year of First Intervention",
    y = "Number of Intersections"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
g <- girafe(
  ggobj = p,
  width_svg = 7, height_svg = 5,
  options = list(
    opts_tooltip(
      opacity = 0.8,
      css = "background-color:black; color:white; padding:10px; border-radius:5px; font-family:sans-serif;"
    ),
    opts_hover_inv(css = "opacity:0.5;"),
    opts_hover(css = "opacity:1;"),
    opts_toolbar(saveaspng = TRUE) 
  )
)
g
```
:::

### Intervention-Specific Rollout

To see how each specific safety measure was rolled out over time, the charts below break down the implementation timeline for each of the nine interventions studied. Each chart shows the number of intersections that received that particular treatment for the first time in a given year. Notice how some interventions, like **Neighborhood Slow Zones**, were implemented heavily towards the beginning of the program's roll-out, while others, like **Street Improvement Corridors**, were deployed throughout the observation period.

While the program's expansion to new intersections paused in 2021, the work itself did not. The charts below reveal a strategic shift: instead of expanding the program's footprint, the city began **deepening the investment** by layering additional safety measures onto intersections that were already part of the program.

```{r plot-intervention-facets, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, fig.height=10, fig.width=9}

first_year_by_intervention <- first_year_by_intervention %>%

    data_id_text = paste(first_year, intervention_type)
  )
p <- ggplot(first_year_by_intervention, aes(x = first_year, y = num_intersections,
                                             tooltip = tooltip_text,
                                             data_id = data_id_text)) +
  geom_col_interactive(fill = "#008080", alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ intervention_type, scales = "free_y", ncol = 3) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) +
  labs(
    title = "First-Year Implementation for Each Vision Zero Intervention",
    x = "Year of First Implementation",
    y = "Number of Intersections Treated"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank()
  )
g <- girafe(
  ggobj = p,
  width_svg = 9, height_svg = 10,
  options = list(
    opts_tooltip(
      opacity = 0.8,
      css = "background-color:black; color:white; padding:10px; border-radius:5px; font-family:sans-serif;"
    ),
    opts_toolbar(saveaspng = TRUE)
  )
)
g
```

### Impact of VZ Interventions on Pedestrian Safety

Instead of just looking at intersections before and after a treatment, our staggered difference-in-difference design does something smarter: it compares the **change in casualties at a treated intersection** to the **change in casualties at similar intersections that *hadn't received that treatment yet***.

We used a negative binomial regression model to estimate the effect of each intervention on the annual count of pedestrian casualties. The results are presented as an **Incidence Rate Ratio (IRR)**. An IRR **below 1.0** suggests the intervention *reduced* casualties, while an IRR **above 1.0** suggests it *increased* them.

The table below summarizes these findings. Rows are colored based on the result: **green** for a statistically significant reduction, **red** for a significant increase, and **grey** for no significant effect.

```{r table-results, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
# Plot and display
regression_results_detailed %>%
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "Impact of VZ Interventions on Pedestrian Casualties"
  ) %>%
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(IRR, P_Value),
    decimals = 3
  ) %>%
  fmt_percent(
    columns = Percent_Change,
    decimals = 2
  ) %>%
  cols_merge_range(
    col_begin = CI_Lower,
    col_end = CI_Upper,
    sep = ", "
  ) %>%
  cols_label(
    Intervention = "Intervention",
    IRR = "IRR",
    CI_Lower = "95% CI for IRR",
    Percent_Change = "% Change",
    CI_Percent_Formatted = "95% CI for % Change",
    P_Value = "p-value"
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = list(cell_fill(color = "#e6f5e6"), cell_text(weight = "bold")),
    locations = cells_body(rows = IRR < 1 & P_Value <= 0.05)
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = list(cell_fill(color = "#fee0e2"), cell_text(weight = "bold")),
    locations = cells_body(rows = IRR > 1 & P_Value <= 0.05)
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = list(cell_fill(color = "#f7f7f7")),
    locations = cells_body(rows = P_Value > 0.05)
  ) %>%
  cols_width(Intervention ~ px(300)) %>%
  tab_options(
    table.border.top.color = "white",
    column_labels.border.bottom.color = "black",
    column_labels.border.bottom.width = px(2)
  )
```

### Ranking Intervention Effectiveness

::::: grid
::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-5}
The bar chart visualizes the estimated percent change in pedestrian casualties for each intervention, providing an at-a-glance summary of which strategies were most effective.

-   **What Works Best?** The most successful interventions manage vehicle speed through physical design or regulation.
    -   Neighborhood Slow Zones **(-18.4%)**
    -   Turn Traffic Calming **(-14.4%)**
    -   Speed Humps **(-11.5%)**

-   **What Doesn't Work (or Makes Things Worse)?**
    -   25 MPH Signal Retiming **(+7.1%)** was the only intervention associated with a harmful effect.
    -   Leading Pedestrian Intervals, Enhanced Crossings, and SIP Intersections had no statistically significant effect.
:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-7}
```{r plot-effects, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, fig.height=6}
# Plot and display
results_with_color <- results_with_color %>%
  mutate(
    tooltip_text = paste0("<b>", str_wrap(Intervention, 30), "</b><br>% Change: ", percent(Percent_Change, accuracy = 0.1))
  )
p <- ggplot(results_with_color, aes(
    x = Percent_Change, 
    y = fct_reorder(str_wrap(Intervention, width = 30), -Percent_Change), 
    fill = Significance,
    tooltip = tooltip_text,
    data_id = Intervention
  )) +
  geom_col_interactive() +
  geom_text(aes(label = percent(Percent_Change, accuracy = 0.1)), 
            hjust = ifelse(results_with_color$Percent_Change > 0, -0.2, 1.2),
            size = 3.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Significant Reduction" = "#2ca25f", 
                               "Significant Increase" = "#de2d26", 
                               "Not Significant" = "grey80"), guide = 'none') +
  scale_x_continuous(
    labels = scales::percent,
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.25, 0.25))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Ranking Intervention Effectiveness",
    subtitle = "Estimated % change in annual pedestrian casualties",
    x = "% Change in Annual Casualties",
    y = ""
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 11),
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5)
  )
g <- girafe(
  ggobj = p,
  width_svg = 8, height_svg = 6,
  options = list(
    opts_tooltip(
      opacity = 0.8,
      use_fill = TRUE, 
      css = "color:white; padding:10px; border-radius:5px; font-family:sans-serif; text-align:center;"
    ),
    opts_hover_inv(css = "opacity:0.5;"),
    opts_hover(css = "opacity:1;"),
    opts_toolbar(saveaspng = TRUE)
  )
)
g
```

### Conclusion & Policy Implications

Our analysis confirms that Vision Zero has had a tangible, positive impact on pedestrian safety, but not all interventions contribute equally. The findings provide a clear mandate for future transportation policy:

-   **Prioritize Speed Management:** The most effective way to protect pedestrians is to control vehicle speed. Future investments should be heavily focused on expanding infrastructure like **Neighborhood Slow Zones**, **Turn Traffic Calming**, and **Speed Humps**.

-   **Re-evaluate Signal Retiming:** The finding that signal retiming to favor vehicle flow is associated with an *increase* in pedestrian casualties is alarming. Transportation agencies must carefully review this practice and consider pairing it with other proven safety measures.

-   **Focus on Systemic, Not Spot, Treatments:** Redesigning an entire street segment (**SIP Corridors**) was effective, while implementing similar projects at a single **intersection** was not. This suggests that creating a consistently safe environment along an entire corridor is more impactful than isolated, spot-based fixes.

Ultimately, this research shows that building a safe transportation system and an efficient one are not conflicting goals. Investments in traffic calming are a core component of an efficient network that is safer and more predictable for all.

### About the Data & Analysis

This analysis was conducted by the NYC Council Data Team using publicly available data from [NYC Open Data](https://opendata.cityofnewyork.us/), including datasets from the NYPD and the Department of Transportation. The full methodology is detailed in our to-be-published manuscript.

While our statistical model controls for many factors, traffic safety is incredibly complex. The findings represent our best estimate of the impact of these specific interventions, but other unmeasured factors could also play a role.
